analysis.one_liner: Bans union membership or union fees as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after introduction it was referred to committee and a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that no employer anywhere could agree, through a union contract, to require workers to join a union or pay union dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job. It covers both private workplaces under the National Labor Relations Act and railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act. Today, states can allow such clauses; 22 do. This bill would ban them in every state. Unions would still have to represent every worker under their contracts, but nonmembers could no longer be charged for that representation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who benefit from a union contract but do not want to join or pay dues would keep the full raises and protections of the contract without paying for it. Employers gain bargaining leverage, since unions that must represent free riders collect less money and have less to spend on organizing and bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who refuse union dues; employers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act to strike the provisions that let employers and unions sign contracts requiring employees to join or pay fees to a union as a condition of employment [S2] [S3].
Amends the Railway Labor Act to strike the paragraph allowing railroad carriers to require union dues or fees, including automatic payroll deduction, as a condition of employment [S2] [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to protect the 'free choice of individual employees' to join or refrain from joining a labor organization [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions lose a major funding stream: they would still be legally required to represent every worker in a bargaining unit but could no longer charge nonmembers fees for it. Unionized employers lose the option of negotiating union-security clauses they may prefer, and unions' reduced resources weaken the bargaining power that has historically lifted wages in unionized workplaces.
analysis.who_pays_short: Labor unions and union-supported wage standards

drawbacks.text: Unions must represent all workers in a bargaining unit, so banning mandatory fees lets workers take union-negotiated wages and protections without paying for them; this free-rider problem can drain union finances and weaken the bargaining that produced those gains [S2] [S3].
The bill overrides voluntary agreements already negotiated between employers and unions, taking away both sides' choice to include union-security terms in their own contracts [S2] [S3].
Right-to-work rules are associated with lower wages in unionized sectors, an honest supporter must weigh against the individual-freedom gain for workers who object to funding unions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real gain here: workers who object to union dues would no longer face losing their job over it. But the cost falls on the institutions that negotiate those wages. Because unions cannot opt out of representing nonmembers, banning fees shrinks union budgets while leaving their legal obligations intact, which tends to erode bargaining strength over time. The bill does not offer unions any offsetting protection. It is a one-sided change that helps individual objectors and employers, while the workers who benefit from union contracts collectively share the risk of a weaker union.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, later sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on November 18, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1] [S5].
Ten House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
On January 4, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, which never acted on it, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers who depend on union-negotiated contracts are better off, since the bill never moved and union-security agreements remained lawful. The bill's single sponsor and small group of cosponsors never got their proposal considered.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban union-security agreements nationwide.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing or markup for the remainder of the 111th Congress.

against.name: 253 of 253 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: The Democratic majority controlled the committee schedule and never brought the bill to the floor; no Democrat cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic majority controlled the committee where the bill was left to die.

industries.note: The bill bans union-security agreements, so unions would keep their legal duty to represent every worker but lose the fees nonmembers now pay, cutting their funding for bargaining and organizing. For the unionized workers whose contracts those fees support, that is a loss; for individual workers who object to dues, it is a gain.

industries.industry: Unionized employers, including railroads and airlines
industries.note: Employers would lose the option of negotiating union-security clauses and railroads would lose dues checkoff, but a union with less money is a weaker bargaining partner, shifting leverage toward employers in contract talks.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and anti-union employer groups
industries.note: A national right-to-work law is the long-standing policy goal of employer-side groups that seek weaker unions; making union security illegal nationwide would remove a threat those groups spend against.
